analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable accessibility standards for airlines so wheelchair users and other disabled passengers can fly with dignity.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 11 senators, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in February 2023 and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would update the 1986 Air Carrier Access Act, which bans disability discrimination on flights but has no private right of action and weak enforcement. It would require the Department of Transportation to write minimum accessibility standards covering boarding equipment, seating, lavatories, accessible announcements, stowage of wheelchairs to prevent damage, and access to airport gates, kiosks, websites, and apps. It would require civil penalties for violations like damaged wheelchairs, denied boarding, or passenger harm, and for the first time let passengers sue airlines and recover damages and attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers with disabilities — wheelchair and scooter users, blind and deaf passengers, and people who need boarding assistance — gain enforceable rights, compensation when a wheelchair is damaged or a passenger is harmed, and a toll-free complaint hotline. The bill's findings specifically note that veterans with disabilities continue to face damaged devices and inaccessible aircraft.

how_it_helps.text: Requires DOT to set minimum standards for boarding and deplaning from personal wheelchairs, seating with in-cabin wheelchair restraints where feasible, lavatories, captioning, and stowage of assistive devices in cargo holds to prevent damage, with existing aircraft required to comply within five years of the rules taking effect.

Requires DOT to assess civil penalties for wheelchair or scooter damage, physical harm or fatal injury during assistance, failure to provide boarding help, and wrongful denial of boarding, and to refer patterns of discrimination to the Department of Justice.

Creates a private right of action so aggrieved passengers can sue in federal court for compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees, without first exhausting administrative remedies — the bill notes the existing law, unlike other civil rights statutes, lacks this remedy.

Requires a toll-free disability assistance hotline, mandatory notice on airline websites and apps about how to file complaints, investigation of complaints within 120 days, and public reporting of disability complaint data.
Extends accessibility standards to airport gates, counters, ticketing areas, kiosks, airline websites, and mobile apps, using Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 as a baseline.

analysis.who_pays: Air carriers, including foreign carriers serving the U.S., bear the cost of retrofitting or replacing aircraft, upgrading airport-facing facilities and digital services, paying civil penalties for violations, and defending lawsuits. Some of that cost could show up in ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Retrofitting existing aircraft to accessible standards within five years could be expensive for airlines, and some costs would likely be passed to all passengers through fares.

The new private right of action with punitive damages and attorney's fees would expose airlines to more litigation, which supporters view as essential enforcement but carriers would contest as excessive.

Some requirements are contingent — for example, in-cabin wheelchair restraints are required only 'if deemed technologically feasible' — so the strength of the final rules would depend on DOT's rulemaking after the bill passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For roughly 27 million Americans with disabilities — and for veterans the bill specifically names — the bill would convert unenforced civil rights promises into standards, penalties, and lawsuits with real teeth. The costs are real: aircraft retrofits and litigation risk for airlines. The bill softens this with phase-in periods (two years for rules, five years for existing aircraft) and feasibility exceptions, so the cost side is deliberate and bounded rather than accidental.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, so it died without a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on February 28, 2023, joined by Senators Duckworth, Markey, Casey, Hassan, and Blumenthal as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that referral is the last action in the bill's history.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill — ten Democrats and one Independent — with no Republican cosponsors listed.
The bill never advanced out of committee and received no floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Air carriers came out ahead: the existing rules with no private right of action and no mandatory civil penalties for wheelchair damage or passenger harm remain in place, and the cost of retrofits, penalties, and litigation was avoided.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eleven cosponsors; her office framed it as closing enforcement gaps that leave wheelchair users and other disabled flyers without remedies.

for.name: Sens. Duckworth, Markey, Casey, Hassan, and Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill a six-sponsor Democratic core on the Commerce Committee's jurisdiction.

for.name: 11 Senate cosponsors (10 D, 1 I)
for.what_they_did: Added their names over the bill's lifetime, all from the Democratic caucus and none from Senate Republicans.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; Chair Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or sent it to the floor; the record shows no committee action after the February 2023 referral.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: No member cosponsored or moved the bill
against.what_they_did: None of the bill's eleven cosponsors was a Republican, leaving it without the cross-party support that often moves a bill through committee.

sides.party_line_note: All eleven cosponsors were Democrats or Independents — ten Democrats and one Independent — with no Republican support recorded, and no committee or floor vote ever tested broader support.

industries.industry: Air carriers (U.S. and foreign airlines serving the U.S.)
industries.note: The bill would require airlines to retrofit aircraft and boarding equipment, meet standards for lavatories, stowage, and digital access, pay mandatory civil penalties for wheelchair damage or passenger harm, and face private damages lawsuits they cannot be sued for under current law. Because the bill died, airlines keep the pre-2023 status quo in which a damaged $30,000 wheelchair draws at most discretionary fines and passengers have no day in court.

Airports and vendors of check-in kiosks, apps, and booking sites would have had to make gates, counters, kiosks, and digital services accessible under standards written by DOT, a compliance cost paired with better access for disabled customers.
